newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's consumer demand set to pick up - study.
newsitem.headline: Canada's consumer demand set to pick up - study.

text.p: Consumer demand in Canada is poised to pick up this year because of a recent boost in employment, wage gains and prevailing low interest rates, according to a report released on Tuesday by an economic research group.
The Conference Board of Canada in its summer outlook projected a 4.5 percent rise in domestic demand this year, based on stronger consumption and a healthy rise in business investment.

The board revised upwards its overall growth projections, predicting 3.1 percent growth in gross domestic product in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998. Previous projections set 1997 GDP growth at 2.9 percent and 2.7 percent in 1998.
"This upturn in overall growth comes at a good time for debt-laden consumers, since it reflects the recent surge in job creation," said Paul Darby, the board's director of economic services.
"Since mid-1996, production has been outpacing job creation and with good prospects for further demand growth, employers are starting to hire."

Canada's strengthening economy has been haunted in recent years by an unemployment rate hovering around 10 percent. But the number of jobs created in the past three months almost matches job creation for all of 1996, the board said.

However, personal savings have dwindled to almost nothing, household debt is at record high levels relative to personal income, confidence remains low and bankruptcies have been soaring, the board cautioned.

While exports are set to remain robust, export growth will likely lag imports in 1997, neutralizing the role of trade in 1998, the report said. Much of Canada's expansion in recent years has been led by exports.
The board said the main risk to its forecast was the possibility of a U.S. hike in interest rates, which would hurt exports and likely weaken the Canadian dollar.
On the fiscal front, the board estimated a federal deficit of C$14.7 billion for the fiscal year that ended on March 31, 1997. Official figures are expected this fall.
The Conference Board forecast a budget deficit of C$5 billion for the current fiscal year and a slight surplus of C$614 million for the 1998-99 fiscal year.
